prompt: A small number of global streaming companies now decide which films and television series are made. Do you think this is a positive or a negative development?
essay:
Commissioning power in film and television has concentrated in a handful of global platforms. I consider this a negative development, despite the fact that more programming is being made now than at any earlier point and that a great deal of it is good.

The gains are obvious and should not be dismissed. Platforms have the capital to fund expensive productions and the reach to turn a series made in Korean or Spanish into a worldwide success, which the older system of national broadcasters and export deals almost never managed. Writers and performers outside the English-speaking world now reach audiences that were previously closed to them, and viewers encounter work they would never otherwise have found. Subtitled drama, once a niche interest in most markets, now routinely reaches the largest audiences on these services, which no national broadcaster ever achieved.

The concern is not volume but the narrowing of the mechanism. When dozens of broadcasters and studios commissioned independently, a project rejected in one place could be taken to another, and the differences between their tastes were what allowed unusual work through. A small number of platforms using similar data and similar measures of success behave more like a single buyer than like many, so a project that fails their test fails everywhere at once. Cancellation after one season, which is common on the platforms, compounds this by making risk expensive for creators as well.

So the industry has more money, more output and fewer doors. I think that combination is negative, because variety in what gets made has always depended on variety in who decides, and that is precisely what has been lost. That is a structural change rather than a temporary one.
title: A few streaming companies choosing what gets made
